s: A 28-year-old man is evaluated for infertility after 2 years of unprotected intercourse. He has had recurrent sinus infections since childhood. Semen analysis shows a low ejaculate volume, acidic pH and no sperm. The vas deferens cannot be palpated on either side, although both testes are normal in size.
l: The missing structures develop from which embryonic structure?
e: Absent vasa deferentia with low-volume, acidic, sperm-free semen describe congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens, classically caused by CFTR mutations, which his sinus infections suggest. The vas deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts all come from the **mesonephric duct**. Without the seminal vesicles the alkaline, fructose-rich fluid is missing too, which is why the volume is low and the pH acidic. The paramesonephric duct forms female internal organs, the urogenital sinus forms the prostate and urethra, and the genital tubercle forms the penis.

w.Paramesonephric duct: The paramesonephric duct regresses in males under AMH and leaves only the appendix testis. It never forms the vas deferens or seminal vesicles.
w.Urogenital sinus: The urogenital sinus forms the bladder, urethra, prostate and bulbourethral glands. It does not form the duct that carries sperm.
w.Genital tubercle: The genital tubercle becomes the glans and shaft of the penis under DHT. It forms no internal duct that carries sperm.
w.Gubernaculum: The gubernaculum guides testicular descent into the scrotum. A defect causes cryptorchidism, not absence of the ducts that carry sperm.

et: Vas deferens, seminal vesicle, ejaculatory duct, epididymis
Lower vagina, Skene and Bartholin glands
Glans and shaft of the penis
bl: The vas deferens, seminal vesicles and ejaculatory ducts come from the mesonephric duct. CFTR mutations can leave them absent.

pt.say: In the Leydig cell box, the Wolffian ducts are listed as epididymis, vas deferens, seminal vesicle and ejaculatory duct, the mesonephric duct derivatives missing here.

s: A 9-month-old boy with normal male external genitalia undergoes surgery for bilateral undescended testes. At laparoscopy, the surgeon finds a small uterus and two fallopian tubes attached to the testes. Karyotype is 46,XY, testicular histology is normal and serum testosterone is appropriate for age.
l: A defect in which signal best explains the internal findings?
e: Normal male external genitalia and a normal testosterone level show that the Leydig cells, the androgen receptor and 5α-reductase all work. What failed is regression of the Müllerian ducts, the job of **anti-Müllerian hormone** from Sertoli cells (or of its receptor). This is persistent Müllerian duct syndrome. The retained uterus and tubes can tether the testes, so it often presents with cryptorchidism. Missing testis-determining factor would give no testis at all, and a lack of testosterone or DHT would undervirilize the genitalia.

w.Testosterone: Testosterone keeps the Wolffian ducts and drives virilization. It does not remove the Müllerian ducts, and this boy's level and genitalia are normal.
w.Dihydrotestosterone: DHT builds the penis, scrotum and prostate. Its lack causes ambiguous genitalia but leaves Müllerian regression intact.
w.Testis-determining factor: Without this signal the gonad would never form Sertoli or Leydig cells, so there would be no AMH and no testosterone at all.
w.Estradiol: Female ducts develop without any estrogen. Estradiol plays no part in whether the Müllerian ducts persist or regress in the fetus.

et: Uterus and tubes persist in a normal boy
Streak gonads, female phenotype with uterus
bl: A uterus in a normally virilized 46,XY boy means absent anti-Müllerian hormone action: persistent Müllerian duct syndrome.

pt.say: The Sertoli cell box shows AMH making the Müllerian ducts regress; without anti-Müllerian hormone the uterus and tubes persist despite normal testosterone.

s: A 14-year-old raised as a girl is brought in because her voice has deepened and her clitoris has enlarged over the past year. At birth she was noted to have a large clitoris and a separate blind vaginal pouch. Examination now shows increasing muscle mass, no breast development and firm gonads in both labioscrotal folds. Karyotype is 46,XY, and pelvic imaging shows no uterus.
l: Deficiency of which enzyme best explains these findings?
e: A 46,XY child who looks female at birth and virilizes at puberty has **5α-reductase** deficiency. Fetal external genitalia need DHT, which this enzyme makes from testosterone in genital skin, so they stay undervirilized. Testosterone itself keeps the Wolffian ducts, and Sertoli cells still make AMH, so the internal ducts are male and there is no uterus. At puberty, adult testosterone levels act on androgen receptors directly. 21-hydroxylase deficiency virilizes 46,XX infants, and 17α-hydroxylase deficiency blocks androgen synthesis altogether.

w.Aromatase: Aromatase converts androgens to estrogens. Its deficiency does not stop DHT from forming in a 46,XY child.
w.21-hydroxylase: 21-hydroxylase deficiency shunts adrenal precursors into androgens, so it virilizes 46,XX infants. Genotypic males look normal at birth.
w.17α-hydroxylase: 17α-hydroxylase deficiency blocks all sex steroid synthesis, so a 46,XY patient stays female with no pubertal virilization. It also causes hypertension and hypokalemia.
w.3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase: 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency blocks adrenal and gonadal steroid synthesis early. It does not leave testosterone free to virilize at puberty.

bl: 46,XY with female genitalia at birth and virilization at puberty means 5α-reductase deficiency: no fetal DHT, intact testosterone.

pt.say: The bottom box of the male column shows 5α-reductase making DHT, the androgen the fetal penis, scrotum and prostate need.

s: A 13-year-old girl who began menstruating 6 months ago has worsening monthly pelvic pain. Her periods are regular. Examination shows normal breast and pubic hair development and a tender bulge in the right lateral vaginal wall. Ultrasound shows no right kidney. MRI shows two separate uterine bodies with two cervices and a right hemivagina distended with blood.
l: Abnormal development of which single embryonic structure best explains both the renal and the genital findings?
e: She has uterus didelphys with an obstructed right hemivagina and renal agenesis on the same side. The ureteric bud sprouts from the **mesonephric duct**, and the paramesonephric duct grows along it. An early mesonephric defect on one side therefore removes the kidney and disturbs fusion of the Müllerian ducts. A paramesonephric defect alone explains the uterus but not the kidney, and a defect of the metanephric mesenchyme explains the kidney but not the uterus. The urogenital sinus and genital ridge form neither organ.

w.Paramesonephric duct: The paramesonephric ducts built the two uteri and cervices, so fusion failed there. A primary Müllerian defect would not explain the missing kidney.
w.Metanephric mesenchyme: The metanephric mesenchyme forms nephrons after the ureteric bud induces it. Its failure alone causes renal agenesis without any Müllerian fusion defect.
w.Urogenital sinus: The urogenital sinus forms the lower vagina and urethra. It does not form the kidney or guide the Müllerian ducts.
w.Genital ridge: The genital ridge forms the gonads, and her normal breasts and regular cycles show that her ovaries formed and work normally.

et: Male ducts; ureteric bud in both sexes
Gives rise to the ureteric bud
bl: Müllerian anomalies with renal agenesis on the same side point to the mesonephric duct, which gives the ureteric bud and guides the Müllerian duct.

hl: The mesonephric duct links kidney and uterus
A hemivagina may obstruct; renal agenesis
pt.say: The band names the mesonephric duct as the link: it sprouts the ureteric bud and guides the Müllerian duct, so a didelphys with an obstructed hemivagina and same-side renal agenesis comes from one early defect.

s: A 32-year-old woman has had three consecutive miscarriages at 9 to 11 weeks' gestation. Parental karyotypes and tests for antiphospholipid antibodies and thyroid disease are normal. Imaging shows two uterine cavities side by side, with one cervix and a smooth, convex external fundal contour.
l: Failure of which developmental step best explains her uterine anomaly?
e: Two cavities with a smooth, convex outer fundus describe a **septate uterus**. The ducts fused normally, but the midline wall between them was never resorbed. It is the most common Müllerian anomaly and the one most linked to recurrent pregnancy loss, because the poorly vascularized septum is a poor place for an embryo to implant. If the ducts had failed to fuse, the result would be a bicornuate uterus with a deep fundal cleft, or didelphys with two cervices. Failure of one duct to form gives a unicornuate uterus.

w.Fusion of the paramesonephric ducts: Partial failure of fusion creates a bicornuate uterus, whose fundus is indented by a deep external cleft. This patient's smooth outer contour rules that out.
w.Formation of one paramesonephric duct: If one duct fails to form, a single horn with one tube remains, a unicornuate uterus, often with renal agenesis on the missing side.
w.Canalization of the vaginal plate: Failed canalization of the vaginal plate blocks the lower tract, causing a transverse vaginal septum or atresia with cyclic pain, not two uterine cavities.
w.Regression of the mesonephric ducts: Persistent mesonephric remnants in females form Gartner duct cysts in the lateral vaginal wall. They do not divide the uterine cavity.

bl: Two cavities with a smooth external fundus mean failed resorption of the midline septum: a septate uterus, the commonest anomaly.

pt.say: The third card shows the step that failed: the midline septum between the fused ducts is not resorbed, leaving a septate uterus with a smooth fundus and two cavities, the most common anomaly.

s: A 16-year-old girl has never had a menstrual period. She has normal breast development and normal pubic and axillary hair. Pelvic examination shows a short, blind-ending vagina. Ultrasound shows normal ovaries but no uterus, and a renal ultrasound shows a pelvic kidney. Karyotype is 46,XX, and serum testosterone is in the normal female range.
l: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
e: A 46,XX patient with normal ovaries, normal breasts and pubic hair, and an absent uterus and upper vagina has **Müllerian agenesis** (Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome). The paramesonephric ducts failed to form, but the ovaries work normally, so puberty proceeds. A renal anomaly is common because the ducts develop alongside the mesonephric system. Complete androgen insensitivity also gives a blind vagina and no uterus, but it comes with a 46,XY karyotype, male-range testosterone and sparse pubic hair. An imperforate hymen and a transverse septum leave the uterus present.

w.Complete androgen insensitivity: Androgen insensitivity also leaves a blind vagina and no uterus, but it needs a 46,XY karyotype with testes, male-range testosterone and sparse pubic hair.
w.Imperforate hymen: An imperforate hymen leaves the uterus intact behind a closed membrane, so blood collects as hematocolpos with cyclic pain and a bulging introitus.
w.Turner syndrome: Turner syndrome (45,X) causes streak ovaries, so estrogen is low and the breasts do not develop. The uterus is present but small.
w.Transverse vaginal septum: A transverse septum blocks the vagina above a normal hymen. The uterus and cervix are present, and menstrual blood collects above the septum.

bl: Primary amenorrhea with normal breasts, normal ovaries, 46,XX and no uterus is Müllerian agenesis, often with renal anomalies.

pt.say: In the first card neither duct forms: Müllerian agenesis (MRKH) is a 46,XX girl with normal ovaries, breasts and pubic hair but no uterus and a short blind vagina, often with a renal anomaly.

s: A 13-year-old girl has had crampy lower abdominal pain for a few days each month for the past 5 months. She has never menstruated. Breast and pubic hair development are Tanner stage 4. Examination shows a tense, bluish, bulging membrane at the introitus, and ultrasound shows a vagina distended with fluid.
e: Cyclic pain without menses, normal puberty and a bulging bluish membrane with blood distending the vagina (hematocolpos) define an **imperforate hymen**. The membrane where the vaginal plate meets the urogenital sinus never opened, so a normal uterus sheds into a closed vagina. Müllerian agenesis and androgen insensitivity have no functioning uterus, so there is no cyclic pain or trapped blood. Vaginal atresia leaves a uterus above a missing lower vagina, with no bulging membrane at the introitus.

w.Müllerian agenesis: Müllerian agenesis removes the uterus and upper vagina, so there is no endometrium to shed. There is no monthly pain and no fluid-filled vagina.
w.Complete androgen insensitivity: Androgen insensitivity gives a 46,XY patient a short blind vagina without a uterus. With no endometrium, blood cannot collect behind the introitus.
w.Vaginal atresia: In vaginal atresia the lower vagina is replaced by fibrous tissue, so blood collects higher up and no thin membrane bulges at the introitus.
w.Gartner duct cyst: A Gartner duct cyst is a mesonephric remnant in the lateral vaginal wall. It does not block menstrual flow.

bl: Primary amenorrhea with cyclic pain and a bulging bluish membrane is an imperforate hymen with hematocolpos.

pt.say: The fourth card shows the vaginal plate failing to open: an imperforate hymen gives a bulging bluish membrane, hematocolpos and cyclic pain, with a normal uterus above the blockage.

s: A full-term male newborn has a urethral opening on the underside of the penile shaft near the penoscrotal junction, a hooded foreskin that is incomplete ventrally, and downward curvature of the penis on erection. Both testes are palpable in the scrotum.
l: Which embryologic failure explains this anomaly?
o: Failure of the urethral folds to fuse
Abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle
Failure of the labioscrotal swellings to fuse
e: A ventral opening with ventral hooding and chordee is **hypospadias**. Under DHT the urethral folds normally fuse from the base toward the glans to enclose the spongy urethra. Incomplete fusion leaves the opening anywhere along the underside. Circumcision is delayed because the foreskin may be needed for repair. Epispadias comes from an abnormally positioned genital tubercle and puts the opening on the top, and unfused labioscrotal swellings give a bifid scrotum.

w.Abnormal positioning of the genital tube: Abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle produces epispadias, a dorsal opening often with bladder exstrophy. It is the mirror image of this ventral defect.
w.Failure of the labioscrotal swellings to: Unfused labioscrotal swellings leave a bifid scrotum. This baby's scrotum holds both testes, and the defect lies in the urethra itself.
w.Persistence of the processus vaginalis: A patent processus vaginalis causes an indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele. It does not affect the urethra.
w.Persistence of the paramesonephric ducts: Retained Müllerian ducts leave a uterus and tubes inside a normally virilized boy. The external urethra develops normally.

et: Failure of the urethral folds to fuse
Abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle
Failure of the labioscrotal swellings to fuse
bl: Hypospadias is failure of the urethral folds to fuse, leaving a ventral meatus. Epispadias is dorsal.

pt.say: The urogenital folds row shows that these folds form the ventral shaft and spongy urethra, so failure of the urethral folds to fuse leaves a ventral opening.

s: A male newborn has an exposed, everted bladder plate on the lower abdominal wall below a low-set umbilicus. The pubic bones are widely separated. The penis is short and broad, with the urethral opening on its upper surface and an open urethral groove running along the dorsum.
l: Which embryologic abnormality best explains the penile finding?
o: Abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle
Failure of the urethral folds to fuse
Failure of the labioscrotal swellings to fuse
e: A dorsal urethral opening is **epispadias**. With an exposed bladder and widely separated pubic bones, it is part of the bladder exstrophy complex. The genital tubercle forms in an abnormal position, and the defective lower abdominal wall leaves the bladder and dorsal urethra open. Failure of the urethral folds to fuse causes hypospadias, a ventral opening. A persistent urachus leaks urine at the umbilicus without exposing the bladder.

w.Failure of the urethral folds to fuse: Unfused urethral folds leave the opening on the underside, which is hypospadias. This infant's opening and groove are on the top of the penis.
w.Failure of the labioscrotal swellings to: Unfused labioscrotal swellings produce a bifid scrotum. That does not open the urethra along the top of the penis.
w.Persistence of the processus vaginalis: A patent processus vaginalis allows an indirect inguinal hernia or hydrocele. It has nothing to do with the bladder or the urethra.
w.Persistence of the urachus: A patent urachus drains urine from an intact bladder through the umbilicus. Here the bladder itself is exposed on the abdominal wall.

et: Abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle
Failure of the urethral folds to fuse
Failure of the labioscrotal swellings to fuse
bl: Epispadias is a dorsal urethral opening from abnormal positioning of the genital tubercle and travels with bladder exstrophy.

pt.say: The epispadias card shows a dorsal urethral opening from a genital tubercle formed in the wrong position, traveling with bladder exstrophy; hypospadias above it is the failure of urethral folds to fuse.

s: A 7-month-old boy has a soft, painless swelling of the right hemiscrotum that is small in the morning and larger by evening or after crying. The swelling transilluminates brightly, the testis is palpable within it, and no bowel sounds are heard over it.
l: Failure of which embryonic structure to close explains this swelling?
e: A transilluminating scrotal swelling that changes size through the day is a communicating hydrocele. Peritoneal fluid flows up and down a patent **processus vaginalis**. This peritoneal pouch runs ahead of the testis through the inguinal canal. Its distal part becomes the tunica vaginalis, and the rest normally closes around birth. If the opening is wider, bowel can follow as an indirect inguinal hernia. The gubernaculum guides descent but is not a hollow channel, and a patent urachus or vitelline duct opens at the umbilicus.

w.Gubernaculum: The gubernaculum is a solid cord that guides the testis into the scrotum. It has no lumen, so it cannot carry peritoneal fluid.
w.Urachus: The urachus connects the bladder dome to the umbilicus. A patent urachus leaks urine at the navel, far from the scrotum and groin.
w.Vitelline duct: The vitelline duct joins the midgut to the yolk sac. Remnants cause a Meckel diverticulum or stool at the umbilicus, not scrotal fluid.
w.Mesonephric duct: The mesonephric duct forms the epididymis and vas deferens, which carry sperm. It has no connection to the peritoneal cavity.

et: Peritoneal pouch through the inguinal canal
Scrotal ligament; ovarian and round ligaments in females
bl: A communicating hydrocele or indirect hernia follows a patent processus vaginalis, the peritoneal pouch that forms the tunica vaginalis.

pt.say: The bottom row shows the processus vaginalis becoming the tunica vaginalis in males; a patent processus vaginalis lets peritoneal fluid reach the scrotum.

s: A 7-month-old boy has an empty left hemiscrotum. The left testis is palpable high in the inguinal canal and cannot be brought down into the scrotum. The right testis is normal. His parents ask about long-term consequences, and a surgeon recommends orchiopexy in the coming months.
l: Which risk will remain increased in this boy even after successful orchiopexy?
o: Germ cell tumor in either testis
Leydig cell tumor of the left testis
Torsion limited to the right testis
e: Cryptorchidism raises the risk of testicular **germ cell tumors**, especially seminoma. The risk persists after orchiopexy and extends to the normally descended testis, which suggests an intrinsic defect of testicular development rather than an effect of position alone. Early orchiopexy improves fertility and makes the testis easy to examine, but it does not remove the cancer risk. Leydig cell tumors are not linked to maldescent, and a unilateral undescended testis usually leaves testosterone production and puberty normal.

w.Leydig cell tumor of the left testis: Leydig cell tumors are rare tumors that secrete androgens. They are not the tumors linked to maldescent, which arise from germ cells.
w.Torsion limited to the right testis: An undescended testis does carry a higher torsion risk, but that risk belongs to the maldescended left side and falls once the testis is fixed in the scrotum.
w.Varicocele of the left testis: A left varicocele comes from impaired drainage of the left testicular vein into the renal vein. It develops in adolescence and is unrelated to descent.
w.Androgen deficiency with delayed puberty: One undescended testis rarely lowers testosterone, because the other testis keeps working and Leydig cells tolerate heat better than germ cells. Puberty usually proceeds normally.

et: Germ cell tumor in either testis
Germ cells, from germ cell neoplasia in situ
Leydig cell tumor of the left testis
Torsion limited to the right testis
bl: Cryptorchidism raises germ cell tumor risk, mainly seminoma, in both testes. Orchiopexy improves fertility but does not remove it.

pt.say: The cryptorchidism card states that germ cell tumor risk, mainly seminoma, stays raised in both testes even after orchiopexy, which improves fertility but does not remove the cancer risk.

s: A 17-year-old girl has primary amenorrhea and no breast development. She is of normal height, and examination shows sparse pubic hair and normal female external genitalia. Ultrasound shows a small uterus and no identifiable ovaries. FSH and LH are markedly elevated. Karyotype is 46,XY, and sequencing shows a loss-of-function mutation in the SRY gene.
l: Failure of which cell type to differentiate best explains why she has a uterus?
e: Without SRY the gonads never become testes and remain streak gonads, so FSH and LH are high and the breasts do not develop. The uterus reflects missing **Sertoli cells**. SRY normally makes the supporting cells become Sertoli cells, and their anti-Müllerian hormone removes the Müllerian ducts. Absent Leydig cells explain the female external genitalia and the missing Wolffian ducts, but androgen lack alone never keeps a uterus. Granulosa and theca cells belong to ovarian follicles, and germ cells do not secrete AMH.

w.Leydig cells: Absent Leydig cells explain the female external genitalia and the missing male ducts. Testosterone does not remove Müllerian ducts, so they cannot explain the uterus.
w.Granulosa cells: Granulosa cells are the ovarian partners of Sertoli cells. The fetal ovary makes little AMH, which is why a normal female keeps her uterus.
w.Primordial germ cells: Germ cells migrate in from the yolk sac and are needed to organize the gonad. They secrete no hormone that controls duct regression.
w.Theca cells: Theca cells surround ovarian follicles and supply androgen for aromatization after puberty. They never make the hormone that removes the Müllerian ducts.

et: Estradiol after puberty; little fetal AMH
bl: In Swyer syndrome, absent SRY means no Sertoli cells and no AMH, so a 46,XY girl keeps a uterus.

pt.say: The first box of the male column shows Sertoli cells secreting AMH; without SRY no Sertoli cells form, so the Müllerian ducts persist as a uterus.
